title: Electrolyser / hydrogen chain
eyebrow: Product-chain pilot · splitting water for fuel
h1: Tiny today, iridium-gated at scale — and the chemistry is the lever
deck: Green-hydrogen electrolysis barely exists yet — a few gigawatts worldwide — but it is growing fast. Its future chokepoint is not the metals people expect: it is iridium, one of Earth's rarest elements, needed by PEM stacks. And that chokepoint is optional, because alkaline electrolysers avoid it entirely.
byline: electricity + water ≠ PEM stack (iridium) vs alkaline stack (nickel) ≠ the hydrogen ≠ ammonia / fuels
correction: The honest reading of this chain is that its material chokepoint is in the future tense. Installed electrolysis is still tiny (a few GW) and today's limits are cost, cheap electricity and actual demand — not minerals. But at the terawatt scale climate plans imply, PEM electrolysers would need far more iridium than is mined. The escape hatch is chemistry: alkaline stacks use nickel, not PGMs.

history.title: Fast growth off a tiny base: installed electrolysis, 2021 → 2025
history.note: IEA Global Hydrogen Review. Installed electrolysis roughly sextupled from 2021 to 2025 — but from ~0.6 to only ~4 GW, a rounding error against the terawatts that net-zero scenarios imagine. The 2025 point is an early estimate. The chart is here to make the scale honest: the hype is large, the built base is not, and the material chokepoint is therefore a future risk, not a present one.

sections.h2: 1 · The base is tiny — so the risk is future-tense

panels.text: After years of announcements, the world has only a few gigawatts of installed electrolysis, and less than 1% of hydrogen is low-emissions. Today's constraints are economic — the cost of electrolysers, cheap enough clean power, and buyers willing to pay a green premium — not a shortage of any metal. The material chokepoint only appears if this scales by orders of magnitude.

panels.h3: Why forecasts here must be marked
panels.text: Almost every alarming 'hydrogen needs X% of world iridium' figure is conditional on a terawatt-scale build-out that has not happened and may not. This chain is the atlas's clearest case for labelling the tense of a claim: the concentration is real in the metal, but the demand behind it is a projection, and is flagged as one.
panels.flag: the demand is a projection, not a fact

sections.h2: 2 · The chokepoint — if it comes — is iridium

panels.h3: PEM stacks need a metal that barely exists
panels.text: Proton-exchange-membrane electrolysers use platinum and, critically, iridium as catalysts. Iridium is among the scarcest elements in the crust, produced as a tiny by-product of platinum mining concentrated in South Africa (see the PGM chain). At terawatt scale, PEM's iridium appetite would collide with a supply measured in a few tonnes a year — a hard geological ceiling.
panels.note: IEA critical-minerals analysis; do not infer iridium demand from platinum loadings.

panels.text: Alkaline electrolysers — the older, mature technology — use nickel-based catalysts and no PGMs at all, and China is building alkaline capacity at scale. So the iridium chokepoint is avoidable by technology choice, at some cost in flexibility. As with wind drivetrains and EV motors, the material risk here is a design decision, not destiny.
panels.flag: nickel, not iridium — a design choice

sections.h2: 3 · What this chain is really waiting on

panels.h3: The near-term limits are not minerals

cards.d: Electrolysis is only as green and as cheap as the electricity feeding it; abundant low-cost renewable power is the real enabler.
Without buyers for green hydrogen, ammonia and steel, capacity sits idle — many announced projects have stalled for lack of offtake.
Electrolyser and green-hydrogen costs must keep falling to compete with fossil hydrogen; that, not iridium, gates the next few years.

trade_intro: BACI carries electrolysers under broad electrical-machinery headings and does not separate PEM from alkaline or isolate iridium (which sits in the shared PGM baskets). Read any trade below as coarse context only — the material story here is a technology-and-scale question, not a customs one.
